title: If you're drawn to one
hookLine: if one door calls you, visit its people and teachers, not only its books: two strangers ask Jesus where he lives
tomorrow: why did the Buddha tell an eager new follower to slow down?

lines: STILL NO IDEA WHAT IT'S LIKE INSIDE.
cards: A stack of books, a podcast at double speed, a folder of saved videos, and still no idea what it's actually like inside. John's Gospel opens a scene right there.
Two disciples of John the Baptist hear him point to Jesus, and they start following him. Jesus turns around. "What seek ye?"
They don't ask a question about God. They ask, in the King James Version, "where dwellest thou?" Where do you live?

teach.b: And John adds the plain detail: "They came and saw where he dwelt, and abode with him that day: for it was about the tenth hour." Not a lecture. An afternoon.

One of the two, Andrew, goes straight to find his brother Simon. A few lines later, Philip tells his friend Nathanael about Jesus of Nazareth, and Nathanael scoffs: "Can there any good thing come out of Nazareth?"
Philip doesn't argue. He uses the same words: "Come and see."

That's how John pictures faith beginning: not with a book, but with time spent close to someone, and then a friend bringing a friend. Christians call this discipleship, following a person and learning by staying near.
Worth repeating to someone tonight: in John, the answer to where do you live isn't an address. It's an invitation. If one tradition is pulling at you, John's two words make a fair plan: go and see.
Books tell you what a tradition says.
Its people show you how it's lived: the food, the silence, the arguments, the welcome. And a visit is humble.

teach.h: GO AS A GUEST, AND STAY.
teach.b: You're a guest in someone's home, so go as one: sit near the back, ask before joining in, and stay the afternoon.

how: In John's Gospel the first followers learn by staying with Jesus, and friends bring friends with the words come and see. A visitor to a service, a sitting or a shared meal goes as a guest: watching first, and asking before joining in.

games.q: what does “if you're drawn to one” mean?
o: giving up your own path for the first group you meet
picking one tradition and reading only its scriptures
feeling pulled toward one tradition, and going to meet its people

games.q: come and see: tap the pairs.
p: went to find his brother Simon
can any good thing come out of Nazareth?

s: the two disciples asked Jesus a question about God
they asked, "where dwellest thou?" he said, "come and see."
in John, the two disciples stayed with Jesus that day
"they came and saw where he dwelt, and abode with him that day."
you can learn a tradition fully from its books
John's answer is a visit: books say what a tradition holds; people show how it's lived.

games.q: a friend loves reading about Sikhism and wonders whether to visit a gurdwara or finish one more book first. what does come and see suggest?
o: go: visit as a guest, sit with the people, see how it's lived.
one more book: know it all before you show up anywhere.
skip the visit; a tradition really lives in its scriptures.
games.why: in John the seekers don't get a reading list; they get an afternoon. come and see, and stay.

practice: Bring to mind one tradition that pulls at you, even a little. Name the wish: to see how it's lived.
Name what's in the way, shyness or not knowing where to go, and then the plan: one gathering, one day, and the first question you'd ask.

wordCard.voice: If you're drawn to one: visit its people and teachers, not only its books. In John, the answer to where do you live is come and see.

orig.note: Greek, John 1:46: come and see, Philip's words to Nathanael.

carryVoice: Something to keep: go and see, and stay the whole afternoon. Day 1702, and a door left open.
